title: Supervision 5 essay
description: Describe the cardiovascular responses during sustained exercise. What limits maximal exercise performance under these conditions?
instructions:
This is the work to hand in for Supervision 5. Write it here in one sitting, the same way you’ll write your essays in the online exam.

  • Time. There’s no time limit, but give yourself about 40 minutes. The clock at the top counts the time you spend writing and tells you when you reach 40 minutes. Spend the first few minutes planning, on paper if you like.
  • Equations. Type simple ones into your text, as you’d write them by hand (× is among the special characters, under Ω). For one with a fraction, use the formula tool, Σ. Say what each equation means, and then use it.
  • Pasting. As in the exam, you can copy and paste within your essay, but you can’t paste in text copied from anywhere else. Write everything in your own words.
  • Diagrams. You can add diagrams, just as you can in the exam. Draw one with Insert drawing (the pencil), or use Insert picture to add a picture, such as a photo of a diagram you drew on paper. Type a caption under it. Your pictures go into the Word document with your essay.
  • Saving. Your essay is saved in this browser as you type, so you won’t lose it if you’re interrupted.
  • When you’ve finished, go to the submission page (the ✓ tile at the bottom right), check your essay and submit it. Then hand it in as described below.

questions.title: Exercise and the circulation
questions.text:
Describe the cardiovascular responses during sustained exercise. What limits maximal exercise performance under these conditions?

Write in continuous prose, with an introduction, paragraphs that each make one point, and a conclusion. Use the equations of the circulation to explain and to argue, with specific examples and numbers from the lectures.
questions.guidance:
Read this after you’ve written your essay, and use it before the supervision to look back over what you wrote. It isn’t a model essay. It sets out the ground a good answer covers, and shows how the equations can carry the argument.

What the title asks. Two things. The first part says “describe”, but the best essays explain each response: what it does, and why the body needs it. The second part needs an argument about what limits maximal exercise, weighing up the evidence for each possible limit. Dr Fraser’s equations join the two halves. In the first, they show how the arterial pressure is kept up while TPR falls. In the second, they show where the ceiling on the cardiac output, and so on the delivery of O2, comes from.

  • The frame. ABP = CO × TPR (flow = pressure difference / resistance for the whole systemic circulation, with RAP close to zero), CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR, and CO = HR × SV. Define each term the first time you use it, and come back to the equations in each paragraph.
  • In the muscles: functional hyperaemia. Blood flow to working muscle rises from 2–3 to over 35 mL min−1 per 100 g, about 17-fold, and the muscle extracts a larger fraction of the O2 it receives. With ABP roughly constant, flow = ΔP / R means the resistance of the muscle’s vessels must fall to about a seventeenth. Because resistance goes with 1/r4 (Poiseuille), its arterioles need only about double their radius (171/4 ≈ 2). In the first 15–20 s (phase I), the K+ released by the muscle’s action potentials (up to about 10 mM outside the cells) hyperpolarises the arteriolar smooth muscle. It stimulates the electrogenic Na+/K+-ATPase, and it increases the conductance of inwardly rectifying K+ channels (KIR). The smooth muscle rests at about −40 mV, well positive to EK, so more K+ flows out. L-type Ca2+ channels close, [Ca2+]i falls, and the smooth muscle relaxes. The muscle pump adds to the flow from the start. In the sustained phase (phase II), K+ still matters, with adrenaline on β2-adrenoceptors, adenosine (which opens KATP channels), NO from red cells and a fall in pH. These overlap, so blocking any one of them changes little.
  • In the whole circulation: TPR falls. Skeletal muscle is about 40% of the body’s mass, and in hard dynamic exercise its blood flow rises from about 1 L/min (20% of the cardiac output) to 20 L/min or more (80–90%). TPR may fall to about 20% of its resting value. By ABP = CO × TPR, if the cardiac output didn’t change, the arterial pressure would fall to a fifth. So the cardiac output must rise about five-fold, from about 5 to about 25 L/min. In exercise, TPR is the term that’s challenged first.
  • How venous return rises five-fold. CO = VR = (MSFP − RAP) / RvR, and RAP can’t fall much below zero, so the change has to come on the venous side. Sympathetic venoconstriction of the capacitance vessels (the venules and small veins hold over half the blood) raises MSFP two- to three-fold, and the muscle pump about halves RvR: 2.5 × 2 = 5. The heart’s part is to pump that extra return without RAP rising. Less vagal and more sympathetic activity (noradrenaline on β1-adrenoceptors) raise its rate and contractility, and Starling’s law matches its output to its filling. In Guyton’s curves (below), both curves move up, and they cross at a cardiac output five times higher, with RAP still close to zero (D). Stimulating the heart alone would only lower RAP, and the output would hardly rise (C).
  • CO = HR × SV. Both terms rise. The heart rate rises (in chapter 1, it climbed steadily from about 84 to about 130 a minute over ten minutes of hard cycling), and the stroke volume is kept up, or increased, by the greater filling and contractility. After a heart transplant, which cuts the heart’s autonomic nerves, the heart rate rises much less in exercise, which shows how much of the rise the nerves provide.
  • Control: feedforward, and a reset baroreflex. Feedback alone couldn’t do this. TPR falls the moment the muscles start working, and a reflex that waited for ABP to fall would always be too late. The medulla receives central command, from the cortex and the cerebellum, and signals from receptors in the muscles and joints. The heart rate rises even before exercise starts, and in the curare experiment an attempted handgrip, with the muscles paralysed, raises the heart rate as much as a real one. Central command resets the baroreflex to a higher set point, so the baroreceptors keep the pressure stable around it rather than opposing the rise. Mean ABP rises a little, mostly as a higher systolic pressure. The pulse pressure widens, because blood runs off faster through the dilated muscles in diastole. With MAP ≈ D + (S − D) / 3 you can show that the mean rises much less than the systolic pressure.
  • Redistribution. Sympathetic vasoconstriction (noradrenaline on α1-adrenoceptors) reduces the flow to tissues that can wait, such as the gut and the kidneys, while the arterioles of the brain and the heart constrict little. Circulating adrenaline dilates the arterioles of skeletal muscle and the heart through β2-adrenoceptors.
  • What limits maximal performance. A useful frame is O2 uptake = cardiac output × the O2 extracted from each litre of blood. That’s the Fick principle, Dr Fraser’s “O2 delivery is flow × concentration” applied to the O2 the tissues take up. With typical figures, 5 L/min × 50 mL/L = 250 mL/min at rest, and 25 L/min × 150 mL/L = 3.75 L/min at maximal effort. The flow rises five-fold and the extraction three-fold, so the flow contributes more. Then take each possible limit. The lungs: in healthy people, breathing extra O2 barely improves performance, so the lungs aren’t the limit. The blood leaving them is already almost saturated, so extra O2 adds little to it. (Raising the blood’s haemoglobin, as blood doping does, does raise the maximal O2 uptake, which fits the delivery of O2 being the limit.) The heart on its own: pacing it faster lowers RAP rather than raising its output, because the cardiac output is capped by venous return. The muscles: cycling with two legs gives less than twice the power and O2 uptake of one leg. Each leg gets less blood, because the resistance of the legs’ vessels rises (sympathetic vasoconstriction, holding ABP up when more muscle is dilating than the cardiac output can supply), and each uses less O2, even though it extracts a greater fraction of what it gets. So the muscles could do more if they had more blood. In fit people, then, the circulation as a whole sets the limit, which is why elite endurance athletes have such high maximal rates of O2 uptake. In the unfit or the ill, the lungs, the heart or the muscles can be the limit instead.
  • ABP is never allowed to fall. Even at maximal effort the mean arterial pressure is held up: you can’t exercise so hard that ABP falls. So the level of activity seems to be regulated centrally, according to what the circulation can supply, and part of the feeling of fatigue must reflect, indirectly, the capacity of the circulation. That matters in heart failure, where the maximal cardiac output is low and fatigue is a prominent feature.
  • For more marks. Be clear about what the equations assume. ABP = CO × TPR takes RAP as zero, TPR is a lumped parameter, and Guyton’s curves are a model (treating the muscle pump and the heart as two pumps in series is another). The one-third rule for MAP depends on the shape of the pressure wave, and at high heart rates, when diastole is short, the mean lies nearer the middle. In long exercise, especially in the heat, more blood goes to the skin to lose heat, and sweating reduces the plasma volume, so MSFP and the stroke volume tend to fall and the heart rate climbs to keep the cardiac output up.

Guyton’s curves at rest and in exercise. The venous return curves (blue) meet the axis at MSFP, and the cardiac function curves (red) show the heart’s output at each RAP. The output is where they cross. At rest that’s A, 5 L/min with RAP close to zero. Stimulating the heart alone moves only the red curve, and it crosses the resting venous return where that curve is flat, at a negative RAP, with little more output (C). Changing the veins alone, by venoconstriction (MSFP × 2.5) and the muscle pump (RvR ÷ 2), moves only the blue curve. The output rises to about 13 L/min, but RAP rises to about 8 mmHg (B). In exercise both curves move, and they cross at 25 L/min with RAP still close to zero (D). The letters follow Dr Fraser’s slide 30, though his B is venoconstriction alone.

Using the equations. Did you define each term? Did the equations organise your answer, or did you quote them once and leave them? Did you put numbers in, such as TPR falling to a fifth, so that the cardiac output must rise five-fold, and MSFP rising 2.5-fold with RvR halved, so that venous return can rise five-fold? Did you use them in the second half, to show why the heart alone can’t raise the cardiac output, and why O2 uptake is limited by the flow?

Against the core criteria. Do you take a position early on? You might argue, for example, that in a fit person maximal performance is limited by the circulation, because the arterial pressure has to be defended while TPR falls, and venous return sets a ceiling on the cardiac output that the heart can’t raise on its own. Does each paragraph make one point, with specific numbers and evidence? Does the conclusion draw the threads together?
